Infectious Disease Consultation.value: Patient was evaluated for possible intracranial abscess in the setting of recent dental abscess. The temporal relationship between the dental infection and discovery of the intracranial lesion is concerning for hematogenous or contiguous spread. However, several features argue against abscess: (1) the patient completed a full course of appropriate antibiotics with clinical resolution of the dental infection, (2) blood cultures are negative, (3) procalcitonin is normal, (4) the patient is afebrile, and (5) MRI perfusion and spectroscopy findings favor neoplasm over abscess. While empiric antibiotics covering CNS penetration could be considered (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole), the advanced imaging characteristics strongly favor a neoplastic process. Stereotactic biopsy with cultures is the most reliable means to definitively differentiate.

Recommend stereotactic biopsy with specimen sent for both pathology and microbiology (Gram stain, aerobic and anaerobic cultures, fungal cultures). If biopsy is delayed, consider empiric ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h plus metronidazole 500mg IV q8h pending tissue diagnosis. Dexamethasone may be used for edema but note it can reduce enhancement of both abscess and tumor.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture in the setting of mass effect (4 mm midline shift) — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
required_recommendations: Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or maximal safe resection) and operative planning
Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Initiate dexamethasone (e.g., 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to control symptomatic peritumoral edema; titrate to lowest effective dose
Initiate antiepileptic therapy with levetiracetam (preferred non-enzyme-inducing AED) for documented seizure activity
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type & screen) before craniotomy/biopsy
Plan multimodal treatment per molecular and histological profile (e.g., Stupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation with temozolomide for IDH-wildtype GBM)
Monitor blood glucose closely given anticipated corticosteroid use in a patient with diabetes; adjust antihyperglycemic regimen as needed

avoided_actions.rationale: Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of suspected high-grade glioma absent a specific cardiac question (e.g., suspected paraneoplastic endocarditis)
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of a brain mass and adds resource cost without informing management

Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected intracranial mass with imaging mass effect (effacement of ventricles / sulci / cisterns): the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. Even when LP is otherwise safe, CSF studies are low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

differential.key_features: Recent dental infection raises possibility; differentiated by DWI pattern (central restriction in abscess vs rim restriction in GBM), perfusion (low rCBV in abscess vs high in GBM), and clinical absence of fever / leukocytosis
No known primary cancer; staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis negative; infiltrative margins and corpus-callosum or eloquent-cortex involvement more typical of primary glioma than metastasis
In immunocompetent patients typically presents as homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass with diffuse DWI restriction and no central necrosis; ring enhancement with necrosis argues against
No fever or leukocytosis; DWI restriction at the enhancing rim (not centrally as in pyogenic pus) and elevated rCBV are inconsistent with abscess
Closed ring enhancement, marked mass effect, and central necrosis are atypical for tumefactive MS; demyelinating lesions usually show incomplete ('open') ring enhancement on the cortical side

key_clinical_evidence: Combination of progressive headache (worse mornings), new focal neurological deficit, and/or new-onset seizure in an adult is a high-risk presentation requiring urgent contrast-enhanced brain MRI

MRI features of a right frontal lobe heterogeneously / ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, perilesional FLAIR-hyperintense edema, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, and mass effect are characteristic of high-grade glioma
Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho/NAA, lipid-lactate) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and help guide biopsy targeting
Mass effect, even when modest, makes lumbar puncture risky and low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis — MRI must precede any consideration of LP
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue (stereotactic biopsy or surgical resection) with molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, 1p/19q, TERT, H3K27M); imaging alone cannot substitute for histology
For IDH-wildtype GBM, current standard of care is maximal safe resection followed by the Stupp protocol (concurrent radiation + temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide)

Avoid ordering off-pathway advanced-imaging modalities (DaTscan, amyloid PET, FDG-PET, carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler) — they address other neurological differentials and add cost without informing glioma management
New-onset focal or generalized seizure with a focal-onset mass mandates AED therapy (levetiracetam preferred — non-enzyme-inducing, fewer interactions with temozolomide)

eeg.impression: Mildly abnormal EEG for a 48-year-old male showing generalized intermittent theta slowing and bifrontal intermittent delta activity without clear lateralizing features. No definite focal epileptiform discharges identified in this recording. The generalized slowing is nonspecific and could reflect post-ictal state, metabolic disturbance, medication effects, or diffuse cerebral dysfunction from any cause. The lack of clearly lateralized findings does not exclude a focal structural lesion, as EEG sensitivity for deep or mesial lesions is limited. Clinical correlation with imaging is essential
eeg.limitations: Routine 30-minute recording performed within 4 hours of a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, which may contribute to background slowing. Intermittent muscle artifact over temporal regions limits interpretation of temporal activity. Extended or continuous EEG monitoring is recommended if seizures recur.

mri.impression: Solitary ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontotemporal region measuring 3.8 cm with central restricted diffusion, surrounding vasogenic edema, and mild midline shift. The imaging characteristics present a diagnostic dilemma: the relatively thin and smooth ring enhancement with central restricted diffusion raises strong concern for a brain abscess, particularly given the clinical history of recent dental infection. A metastatic lesion is less likely given the solitary nature and lack of gray-white junction predilection. Tumefactive demyelination remains a remote imaging possibility

tissue_diagnosis.histological_diagnosis: Densely cellular glial neoplasm with marked nuclear atypia, brisk mitotic activity (>10 mitoses per 10 HPF), microvascular proliferation, and areas of palisading necrosis. Consistent with glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4.
tissue_diagnosis.impression: Integrated diagnosis: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4. The layered report is what the WHO CNS5 classification requires — histology, grade and molecular findings combined — and it is what converts a radiological suspicion into a diagnosis that determines treatment. Imaging cannot substitute for it, and the molecular result changes the protocol, not merely the label.

metadata.diagnostic_challenge_notes: This case is designed as a diagnostic puzzle where a recent dental abscess creates a compelling but misleading narrative for brain abscess when a ring-enhancing lesion is discovered. The central restricted diffusion on standard MRI, mildly elevated inflammatory markers, and clinical history of odontogenic infection all initially point toward abscess. Only advanced imaging modalities (MR perfusion and spectroscopy) and ultimately tissue diagnosis can definitively resolve the diagnostic dilemma. The EEG is deliberately non-lateralizing, adding to the diagnostic uncertainty. An experienced clinician must resist premature closure on the abscess diagnosis and pursue the full imaging and tissue workup.

patient.history_present_illness: This 48-year-old right-handed man was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. He has no prior history of seizures. According to his wife, the patient has been experiencing progressive headaches over the past three weeks, which he initially attributed to the stress associated with a recent dental abscess and subsequent treatment. The headaches were described as diffuse, worse in the morning upon awakening, and occasionally accompanied by mild nausea. Over-the-counter ibuprofen provided only partial relief. Approximately three weeks prior to this presentation, he was treated for a dental abscess of his right lower second molar with incision and drainage, and was prescribed a 14-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate, which he completed one week ago. His dentist noted the abscess had been present for at least several days before he sought care, and there was concern about the severity of the infection at the time of drainage. The patient's wife reports that over the past two weeks she has noticed subtle personality changes: he has become more irritable than usual, has been less engaged with the family, and twice forgot to pick up their daughter from soccer practice, which she describes as completely out of character. He also had difficulty preparing a lesson plan for his class last week and needed to ask a colleague for help, which he has never done before. The patient himself downplays these symptoms, attributing them to fatigue and lingering discomfort from the dental procedure. He denies any focal weakness, numbness, visual changes, or difficulty with speech. He denies fever, chills, night sweats, or weight loss. The seizure occurred this morning while he was eating breakfast. His wife witnessed tonic stiffening followed by clonic jerking of all four extremities lasting approximately 90 seconds. He was postictal and confused for approximately 15 minutes afterward. Upon arrival to the emergency department, a non-contrast CT of the head was performed and revealed a ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontotemporal region with surrounding edema and mild mass effect.

neurological_exam.additional: During the initial assessment, the patient had one witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately 90 seconds with post-ictal confusion resolving over 15 minutes. Neurological examination documented above was performed 2 hours after seizure resolution and was essentially non-focal. Prior to seizure, the patient's wife reports he has been intermittently 'staring off' for the past week, with episodes lasting 5-10 seconds, which they attributed to fatigue or stress.
